newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean petrol prices seen rise after deregulation.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean petrol prices seen rise after deregulation.

text.p: Petrol prices at South Korean pumps, which jumped 12 percent last week, are set to rise again after January 1 when the government frees oil products from price controls, analysts said.
Beleaguered domestic oil refiners -- fighting to stave off losses -- could seize the opportunity to hike prices by as much as five percent, said George Goundry, an oil analyst at HG Asia.
But a price war to gain market share is unlikely, analysts said.
"Prices will go up," Goundry said. Any increases above five percent could meet resistance from the government, however, which retains the right to intervene if prices become too volatile, he said.
The government raised petrol prices by 12 percent to 815 won ($0.97) a litre last week from 727 won, the first time prices have gone over the 800 won level and the biggest hike since 1992.
The move was aimed at conserving energy and narrowing the current account deficit.

Analysts said further price hikes after the New Year could be limited by a consumer backlash against refiners, whose profits have been hit by a product glut in Asia and foreign exchange losses just as they are embarking on huge capacity expansions.

"The main problem lies in whether the refining industry will be able to withstand pressure from consumer groups and the government regarding inflation," said Yong Han, an energy analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.
From January 1, 1997, domestic prices of gasoline, kerosene, diesel and C-type fuel will be deregulated and no longer subject to a government-set monthly price ceiling.
In the first six months after price controls are lifted, oil refiners must give the government advance notice of price changes on gasoline, kerosene and diesel.
After that, simple notification after the fact is needed.

But the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said it would intervene if prices became too volatile and endanger the stability of the economy. Refiners found guilty of price-fixing or of setting prices artificially low to grab market share would be punished according to the Fair Trade Act.
Han said a price war between refiners was unlikely.

Refiners had spent heavily on capacity expansion and all needed extra revenue to recoup costs. In addition, they have suffered massive currency losses from the rise of the dollar against the local won.
The won has lost about eight percent this year, adding to the import cost of crude.

Several analysts estimated the nation's five oil refiners will lose a combined 350 billion won ($415 million) this year, against an 8.45 billion won shortfall last year. Foreign exchange losses would account for 70 percent of the losses.
Goundry said price rises at the pumps would reflect investment by refiners in filling stations.
"Oil firms have pumped money into gas stations to strengthen their distribution networks. They would include these factors into prices," he said.

"No one is used to the new system," said Kim Sang-bae, an energy analyst at Ssangyong Investment Securities. "They don't want to make a wrong move and get into trouble. They'll watch the market carefully before raising prices."
Also to be deregulated next year are imports and exports of oil products as well as oil product sales, which will no longer be the sole domain of refiners.
Traders with storage facilities will be allowed to import and export crude and oil products without government approval. Storage facilities must be sufficient to hold 60 days of sales volume.
